transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I guess… I came in because I’ve been having these thoughts, and I don’t like saying it out loud, but I keep thinking maybe my family would be better off if I just didn’t wake up. It scared me. I told my supervisor, which was embarrassing because I’m usually the one keeping things running, you know, making sure everybody else is where they’re supposed to be… but I said it, and now I’m here.
Are you wanting to die right now?

I don’t know that I want to die right this second… it’s more that I keep getting this thought, like my family might be better off if I just didn’t wake up. And that scared me enough that I told my supervisor, which I don’t usually do — I usually just keep things moving at work, make sure everybody else is handled. But yeah, those thoughts are why I came in.
Have you been feeling depressed most days?

I’m not sure how to answer “most days.” Some days I feel pretty low, yeah, but then I’ll get busy at work and sort of shove it aside. I mean, there’s always something—someone calling in, schedules changing, some little fire to put out—and then I don’t really stop long enough to name what I’m feeling. So… I guess I’ve felt down, but I don’t know if I’d say most days exactly.
Before this recent period, have you ever gone through another time in your life when you felt depressed like this for a couple of weeks or longer?

Yeah… I think so. Looking back, it’s been kind of coming and going for about a year now, these low stretches. I didn’t really call it that at the time—I’d just say I was tired or had too much going on.

But this one, after my daughter left… this has been the hardest one. It just kind of settled on me more than the others.
Did this current low period start after your daughter left home?

Yeah… pretty much. It was after she left Georgia for the military. I guess I didn’t notice it all at once, you know, because there was a lot going on, getting her ready and trying to act like I was fine with it. But this whole change in me has been about two weeks now since she left.
Since your daughter left, have you still been able to enjoy things you usually like?

Not like I used to, no. I mean, I’ve got tomato plants out there I normally mess with, and I’ll go look at them and just… not care much. Same with sanding wood at my bench. I used to lose time doing that.

And Sundays, I’d usually hang around after church talking to folks, or watch the Falcons and get all worked up at the TV. Lately it’s like I’m looking at all those things and they belong to somebody else. Like I know I’m supposed to enjoy them, but I just don’t feel it.
Since your daughter left, how has your sleep been?

Sleep? Uh… I don’t know, I guess I haven’t really been keeping track of it. Some nights I’m in bed and I’ll think I slept, but then I’m not sure how much of it was real sleep.

I used to just wear myself out enough from work and fooling around in the yard that I’d drop off. My wife used to say I could fall asleep with the TV blaring, especially during those late games. But lately… I don’t know. It’s been different, I think, but I couldn’t tell you exactly.
Since your daughter left, has your appetite changed?

Yeah… it has, I guess. I don’t really get hungry like I should. Most days I have to kind of make myself eat a few bites, and then I’ll just leave the rest sitting there.

Like at the warehouse, somebody’ll bring in something I usually like, or my wife makes food at home, and I look at it and think, “I ought to eat that,” but it just sits there till I end up tossing it. Which feels wasteful, and I was raised not to do that, my mama would’ve had a fit… but yeah, I’m not eating much.
Have you ever tried to kill yourself?

I haven’t done anything like that… I mean, I didn’t come in because I took pills or anything. It’s more that I keep having these thoughts, like maybe my family would be better off if I just didn’t wake up.

And I know that sounds awful to say out loud. I was at work, and I couldn’t shake it, and I finally told my supervisor because it scared me. I didn’t know what else to do.
Have you thought about a specific way you might kill yourself?

No… not a way like that. It’s not like I sat there and picked something out or made some plan. It’s more this thing that keeps coming up in my head, like my family might be better off if I just didn’t wake up.

And I know that’s not a normal thing to be thinking. I was at work when it really scared me, and I ended up telling my supervisor, which I don’t usually do… I mean, I’m not one to go telling people my business. But it got to where I didn’t know what else to do.
Lately, have you been feeling like you’re a burden to your family or that you’ve let them down?

Yeah… I do. I keep turning it over in my head, especially about my daughter leaving. I start thinking I must’ve done something wrong, you know, like if I’d been a better father maybe she wouldn’t have gone, or I would’ve known what to say.

And then I’ll think back on little things, stupid things even, like times I worked late or didn’t understand what she was trying to tell me… I don’t know. My wife says I can’t put it all on myself, but it feels like I let her down somehow.
Since your daughter left, have you been moving or speaking noticeably slower than usual?

Yeah… I think so. People at work keep asking me if I’m sick, and I didn’t even realize it was that noticeable at first.

I’ll be walking down the hall and it’s like I’m going through mud or something. And when somebody asks me a simple question, I just… it takes me forever to answer. I hate that, because I’m supposed to be the one keeping things moving, you know, and now they’re looking at me like something’s wrong.
Before your daughter left, was there ever another time in the past year when these symptoms stayed together for at least two weeks?

Yeah… I mean, if I’m looking back, these low spells have kind of been coming and going for maybe about a year now. It’s hard to pin down, because time gets all mixed up when you’re just trying to get through work and come home and do the regular things.

But this one, after my daughter left… this has been the worst one. The others were there, I think, but not like this.
Have you ever had a period where you felt unusually energetic or wired and needed much less sleep than usual?

Yeah… there was a stretch like that. I don’t know if I’d call it “wired,” exactly, but I had a lot of energy, more than made sense.

I’d be up before daylight, already thinking through changes at the warehouse—moving this, fixing that, how to make things run better. Then I’d come home and start cleaning the garage, and I’d jump from one thing to another like I couldn’t just sit down. My wife would be saying something about one project and I’d already be onto the next one. It felt like I didn’t really want to stop.
During that high-energy stretch, did you feel unusually up or overly confident compared with your normal self?

Yeah… yeah, I did. I mean, I don’t usually go around saying I’m the smartest guy in the building or anything like that. I’m more of a just-get-it-done person.

But during that stretch I really had it in my head that I was about to be regional director, like it was basically obvious. And I kept thinking nobody in the company understood operations the way I did. Like if they’d just listen to me, everything would run right.

Which… saying it now, it sounds kind of big-headed. My wife would give me that look, you know, like, “Who are you talking like?” But at the time it didn’t feel strange to me. It felt true.
During that high-energy stretch, did you need less sleep than usual?

I’m not totally sure, to be honest. I mean, I know I was up earlier, moving around more, but whether I actually needed less sleep… I don’t know how to measure that.

My sleep has never been perfect anyway. Some nights I’m just thinking about work stuff, or I hear a noise and then I’m up, and once I’m up I start making coffee or looking at the garage, and then one thing turns into another. So… maybe? But I can’t say for sure that I was sleeping less and fine with it. I just remember being up and doing things.
During that high-energy stretch, were you talking more than usual?

I don’t know… maybe some? My wife might say I was, because she says I get going and don’t leave much room for anybody else.

But I can be like that at work anyway, you know? In operations you’re always talking—telling one guy where the shipment goes, asking another why the dock door’s tied up, then somebody’s got a problem with the schedule. So it’s hard for me to tell if I was talking more than usual or just had more to say because I was thinking about all these fixes.

I remember explaining stuff a lot, probably repeating myself. But I couldn’t swear it was some huge change.
During that high-energy stretch, were you taking on a lot more projects or staying unusually busy compared with your normal self?

Yeah, I guess that part was pretty clear. I was… I was taking on a lot. Like at work I’d be calling supervisors after hours, telling them about changes I wanted done, new ways to run the shifts, stuff that probably could’ve waited until morning.

And then I’d come home and start drawing up plans, not just for work but for the house too. Like, one minute I’m sketching out a new work schedule, next thing I’m in the garage thinking I should reorganize the whole thing, or fix something in the yard. My wife kept saying, “Can one thing just be one thing?” because I’d start three different projects before finishing the first.

It felt like every idea had to be handled right then, like if I didn’t jump on it, it would get lost or somebody else would mess it up. Looking back, yeah, I was busier than normal.
During that high-energy stretch, were you hospitalized because of it?

Hospitalized? No… I mean, not that I remember. Nobody took me anywhere like that.

I’ve been in hospitals for other people plenty, you know, my father had a thing years back and you end up sitting in those chairs for hours, vending machine coffee, all that. But for that stretch you’re asking about, no, I was still going to work and coming home. My wife was upset with me, sure, but it didn’t turn into… like an ambulance or being admitted or anything like that.
About that high-energy stretch, how long did it last?

I’m not real sure, honestly. Time kind of blurs when I think back on it.

It wasn’t like one afternoon and then done, but I don’t want to give you some exact number and be wrong. My wife would probably have a better handle on it, because she remembers that kind of thing better than I do. I just remember there was a stretch where I was “on,” you know, and then later it wasn’t like that anymore.

I’d have to think about it or ask her.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about being more talkative than usual during the high-energy stretch, but the provided symptom profile does not include a talkativeness or pressured-speech item.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… maybe some? My wife might say I was, because she says I get going and don’t leave much room for anybody else.

But I can be like that at work anyway, you know? In operations you’re always talking—telling one guy where the shipment goes, asking another why the dock door’s tied up, then somebody’s got a problem with the schedule. So it’s hard for me to tell if I was talking more than usual or just had more to say because I was thinking about all these fixes.

I remember explaining stuff a lot, probably repeating myself. But I couldn’t swear it was some huge change.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior high-energy period included increased goal-directed activity, a key manic/hypomanic symptom that would help distinguish bipolar disorder from recurrent or single-episode depression/adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: During that high-energy stretch, were you taking on a lot more projects or staying unusually busy compared with your normal self?

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I was calling supervisors after hours, drawing up new work plans, and starting home projects all at once like every idea had to be handled right then.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether, during the high-energy stretch, there was increased goal-directed activity such as taking on more projects and staying unusually busy.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I guess that part was pretty clear. I was… I was taking on a lot. Like at work I’d be calling supervisors after hours, telling them about changes I wanted done, new ways to run the shifts, stuff that probably could’ve waited until morning.

And then I’d come home and start drawing up plans, not just for work but for the house too. Like, one minute I’m sketching out a new work schedule, next thing I’m in the garage thinking I should reorganize the whole thing, or fix something in the yard. My wife kept saying, “Can one thing just be one thing?” because I’d start three different projects before finishing the first.

It felt like every idea had to be handled right then, like if I didn’t jump on it, it would get lost or somebody else would mess it up. Looking back, yeah, I was busier than normal.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the prior high-energy episode caused marked impairment requiring hospitalization, which best distinguishes bipolar I disorder from major depressive disorder or bipolar-spectrum alternatives.
doctor.question: During that high-energy stretch, were you hospitalized because of it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically whether the high-energy stretch led to hospitalization, but the symptom profile does not include hospitalization or manic-episode severity requiring inpatient care.

patient.answer:
Hospitalized? No… I mean, not that I remember. Nobody took me anywhere like that.

I’ve been in hospitals for other people plenty, you know, my father had a thing years back and you end up sitting in those chairs for hours, vending machine coffee, all that. But for that stretch you’re asking about, no, I was still going to work and coming home. My wife was upset with me, sure, but it didn’t turn into… like an ambulance or being admitted or anything like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the past high-energy episode included markedly increased goal-directed activity lasting long enough to support bipolar disorder over unipolar depression or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: About that high-energy stretch, how long did it last?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the high-energy stretch, but the provided duration items describe depressive/low-period timing rather than the length of the high-energy episode.

patient.answer:
I’m not real sure, honestly. Time kind of blurs when I think back on it.

It wasn’t like one afternoon and then done, but I don’t want to give you some exact number and be wrong. My wife would probably have a better handle on it, because she remembers that kind of thing better than I do. I just remember there was a stretch where I was “on,” you know, and then later it wasn’t like that anymore.

I’d have to think about it or ask her.
